sections.overview: The African savanna elephant is an immensely large herbivore whose movement and feeding shape its surroundings while it depends on broad access to forage and water. It occurs mainly in eastern and southern sub-Saharan Africa, across open grasslands, scrub, and woodland mosaics rather than one uniform kind of savanna. It is a distinct species from the African forest elephant, Loxodonta cyclotis, which is generally smaller and adapted to closed forest; individuals in the forest–savanna transition can show mixed traits.
sections.identification: Adults have grey, deeply folded skin, very large triangular ears, a concave or saddle-shaped back, and a long trunk; these traits together help distinguish them from the smaller, round-eared forest species. A SANParks comparison guide lists broad adult-male ranges of 3–4 m at the shoulder and 4–6.3 tonnes; females are smaller, and size varies with age and population. Known-age Amboseli data were fitted with growth curves: the estimated sex difference widened after about ten years, with males 60–70 cm taller at age 65. The trunk is an elongated upper lip and nose made of muscle, connective tissue, nerves and skin, with no bones; it smells, breathes, touches, lifts and manipulates food. Its sensitive tip has two small opposing projections, often called fingers, which pinch small objects while the flexible trunk can also wrap around larger loads. Tusks are enlarged upper incisors, not horns; both sexes generally grow them, and males tend to have thicker, faster-growing tusks. Some populations show local exceptions: in Gorongosa, Mozambique, ivory poaching during the civil war favored female tusklessness, and researchers implicated tooth-development genes. San Diego Zoo references average adult masses of about 2.8 tonnes for females and 6.0 tonnes for males, with shoulder heights of 2.5–3.0 m and 2.9–3.7 m respectively. Body size varies by population; no standard body-width measurement is reported.
sections.habitat: The species uses grassland, savanna, scrub, and open woodland, shifting among them as seasonal rains change the availability of grass, leaves, and surface water. In arid regions, waterholes anchor dry-season movements, and ranges expand when local forage and water become scarce. Their large ears help limit overheating: flapping moves air across the broad surface and exposes blood vessels on the inner surface of the ear flap, increasing heat loss.
sections.diet: It grazes grasses and sedges, and browses leaves, herbs, fruits, roots, twigs and bark as seasonal plant growth changes. The trunk gathers vegetation and carries it to the mouth, pinching small pieces and wrapping around larger bundles. Unlike a cow, an elephant does not ferment food in a multi-chambered foregut before digestion; microbes ferment fibrous material in the large intestine, after the small intestine. This hindgut fermentation lets food pass relatively quickly, supporting the enormous daily intake needed by a very large body, but it extracts nutrients less completely than slow retention would; elephants compensate by eating for many hours and selecting high-quality parts when available.
sections.behavior: Females and dependent young form enduring family units, usually led by a matriarch; female group membership follows close maternal kinship and affiliative ties. These units do not remain in one fixed herd: related families may gather into larger clans, then separate into smaller parties and reunite as local conditions change, a pattern called fission–fusion. Older daughters and other females help guard and guide calves, spreading care and learned behaviour through the maternal family. Males leave the natal family as they mature and often travel alone or associate in loose bachelor groups; they still encounter female groups, especially when females are receptive. Adult bulls may enter musth, a recurring reproductive state marked by raised testosterone, urine dribbling, secretion from temporal glands and altered behaviour; it can improve access to mates, but sexual activity also occurs outside musth. Communication is multimodal: contact, posture, scent and calls work together, and low rumbles include infrasound, frequencies below human hearing that can carry social signals across open country. Experiments with recorded calls show that females can recognize familiar family voices at long range, while the exact information carried by each call depends on context.
sections.reproduction: Females usually produce one calf after a gestation of about 22 months, among the longest pregnancies of any land mammal. At birth a calf already weighs around 100 kg, and field observations show that healthy newborns generally stand and begin walking within hours, allowing them to keep pace with the family. The mother nurses for years; weaning is gradual and varies, often overlapping with a later birth rather than occurring at one fixed age. Calves learn by following and imitating adults: using the trunk to grasp, drink and feed takes practice, while allomothers provide protection and opportunities to learn social rules. Females commonly wait several years between births because pregnancy, lactation and care require sustained investment; drought and poor body condition can lengthen the interval. Males mature physically later than females and their reproductive success is strongly affected by body size, age and the competitive advantage of musth, so reaching adulthood does not mean immediate breeding access.
sections.ecology: By browsing, grazing, pushing over trees and opening paths, elephants alter vegetation structure; the outcome depends on elephant density, rainfall, soils and the plants present, so local woodland change is not a universal result. In Hwange, elephant density was higher where artificial waterholes were more concentrated in the late dry season; density did not predict short-term vegetation heterogeneity, while long-term waterhole maintenance was associated with less woody structural variety. Elephants also move seeds in dung: in a southern African study of Balanites maughamii, seeds passed through elephant dung germinated better than intact seeds, illustrating one documented plant relationship rather than a rule for every species. In South African Sand Forest, field research found that elephant effects on smaller browsers changed with hillslope position, showing why plant-eater interactions depend on local terrain.
sections.conservation: The IUCN assessed the savanna elephant separately on 13 November 2020 and published the assessment in 2021; a 2022 amendment retained the Endangered category. Earlier IUCN assessments treated African elephants as one taxon: it was listed as Vulnerable in the 2004 and 2008 updates, and Endangered in 1996 under older criteria. The amended assessment identifies continuing ivory poaching and human-driven habitat loss as major drivers, while noting uneven trends: some subpopulations are stable or increasing and others decline faster.
